#5877. China’s Economics of Denial

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Oliver Melton is a Director with Rhodium Group’s China practice.

Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads its research on China’s economy and financial markets. He is the author of the book Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World.

Beijing’s Theory of Success in the Face of Failure

China has correctly diagnosed its most pressing economic problems. The Chinese Communist Party has acknowledged that its economy relies too much on investment and exports and that persistently weak household consumption is the core threat to future growth. The leadership also knows that this imbalanced growth model is causing trade friction with developed and emerging economies alike and will continue to do so. They know there is a growing chorus of economists (including many quiet voices in China) raising the alarm that, if Beijing does not make major changes soon, China will face ever-slower growth, cascading trade disputes, and potentially stagnating household income.

But what is puzzling is that the country’s leaders are not acting. Beijing has announced only modest plans to boost household consumption and domestic demand, and its overall economic strategy remains essentially unchanged—focused on expanding investment in manufacturing, especially in advanced technologies and new strategic industries.

Theories abound as to why Beijing has chosen to ignore the warnings. Many speculate that Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not receiving accurate information or that he and his closest allies have abandoned development as a priority in favor of national security goals or a desire to control the commanding heights of global industry. Others argue that Beijing knows what it should do, but political or institutional constraints prevent it from taking decisive action.

In truth, while these factors all play a part in shaping policy, the real explanation is far simpler. The party is sticking to this path because the leadership believes it is working. It sees the same troubling data—including rising external surpluses, weak consumption, slower household income growth, weak credit demand, rising unemployment and underemployment, and persistent deflation—but it has reached wildly different conclusions about what these developments indicate and what Beijing should do in response.

Chinese economic policy is nested within a methodical planning process, which is meant to ensure that short-term pressures do not distract from long-term priorities. The problem is that the long-term strategy is predicated on the belief that control of advanced technologies and industry will trigger a new round of high-speed growth. This economic strategy can best be understood as a Marxism-infused misapplication of neoclassical economic development theory: Beijing is obsessed with control over technology and physical capital and believes that its ultrahigh levels of investment will accelerate productivity gains and wage growth. But a disproportionate focus on manufacturing and technology cannot increase productivity or wages if those investments are decoupled from the needs of the market and trends in aggregate final demand. This is especially true in a country as large as China—already the world’s largest exporter—that cannot rely on further exports to fuel growth.

China’s worldview treats development as equivalent to capital accumulation and sees productivity as determined by the control and deployment of technology. It posits that the growth of the service sector, higher wages, and higher consumption are the consequences of that physical underlying foundation—they follow naturally in later stages of the development process once the productive industries have flourished. In this conception of economic development, the right strategy is always more investment, more industry, and more technology. The role of the state is to ensure that household savings and industrial profits are recycled through the state-owned banking system or government-guided capital into priority investments rather than frivolous activities, such as services or consumption. The resulting structural imbalance that weakens household income growth, the service sector, and public services was thus not an accident; in China’s economic development theory, this is seen as self-discipline that will pay off with more rapid long-term development.

A key corollary to this view is that the government’s macroeconomic management must guide resource allocation proactively through hands-on intervention, not impassively through interest rates and exchange rates. The state can harness the dynamism and ambition of markets to promote efficiency and innovation in defined spaces, but it is the government’s job to identify the correct focal points for investment to ensure that priority sectors grow at maximum speed and then to intervene to ameliorate imbalances when they inevitably arise.

In this conception of macroeconomics, the economy consists of a massive input-output table where every cell in the matrix is a sector that consumes other cells’ outputs and provides inputs to other producers. If there is an imbalance in supply or demand for certain products—which becomes evident in high or low prices—it may be because of overinvestment in the producing sector or underinvestment in downstream consuming sectors. Government policy seeks to increase output and steadily lower prices by facilitating investment and production throughout the matrix, adjusting the pace and balance of resource allocation as needed if one cell’s output exceeds the demands of the others. The goal is not to develop overcapacity or low profitability in these targeted sectors, but the optimal path for rapid development will inevitably push sectors in that direction.

Beijing has followed this playbook closely. When, for instance, the real estate sector collapsed in 2022 and the structural imbalances in China’s economy became too big to ignore, Beijing responded by increasing its efforts to micromanage credit flows, reversing experiments with interest rate liberalization and financial market reforms while tightening oversight of capital markets and industrial policy funding. Central bank relending facilities now channel low-cost bank loans to prioritize industrial upgrading and equipment purchases for targeted sectors. Thousands of government-run equity funds provide low-cost capital to firms that support a web of industrial and technology strategies. State-owned enterprises intervene to help boost valuations in the stock market, and regulators prioritize firms in strategic sectors for new listings. When a sector is overinvested, policy campaigns such as “anti-involution”—a neologism that describes a basket of discordant policies to resolve overcapacity—are deployed to slow future investment, buttress profitability by fixing prices, or set standards to restrict market entry in a bid to slow output while the other cells in the input-output tables catch up and restore balance over time.

Although hard to comprehend in the context of a market economy, some aspects of this approach have an understandable internal logic in China, especially at a micro level. The collapse of the property sector—roughly a quarter of GDP at its peak—sent massive shock waves through very specific supply and demand pathways in the economy. It made sense for Beijing to calibrate policy for the affected sectors and think in terms of input-output tables as it designed its responses. The frequency of bubbles in China’s equity, commodity, and property markets over the past 15 years has left policymakers deeply wary of accommodative monetary policy for the entire economy, which helps explain why they are experimenting with more targeted tools aimed at specific sectors.

Likewise, a certain level of triumphalism in Beijing is understandable, given that Chinese companies are breaking into pole positions in major conventional industries, such as autos and telecommunications, and many others are poised to thrive in cutting-edge sectors, such as robotics and biotechnology—all in the wake of a massive hit to GDP. For a generation of economic policymakers who cut their teeth trying to revitalize a moribund planned economy in the 1990s and the first decade of this century, the emergence of world-leading (often private) firms is definitive evidence that Beijing has found a winning recipe. From this perspective, Beijing is also dismissive of foreign complaints about unfair market interventions or trade imbalances as the sour grapes of rich countries that had grown accustomed to rent-seeking technology monopolies.

China’s leaders also see some deflation as the fruits of hard-won efficiency gains: the elimination of bottlenecks, economies of scale in manufacturing clusters, construction of world-class infrastructure, improved logistics, and removal of market barriers that have lowered costs up and down manufacturing supply chains. One-off cost reductions from efficiency gains or the abrupt loss of construction activity must be digested by the economy, they would argue, not offset by stimulus. And while foreign commentators and dignitaries warn of growing trade pushback, the data tells a surprisingly different story: China’s export growth barely slowed as the Trump administration imposed sweeping duties and the European Union set up defenses against a handful of sectors, such as electric vehicles.

The core problem with China’s economic strategy, however, is that aggregate domestic demand consistently falls far short of domestic supply. Chinese planners’ input-output tables will not balance unless domestic workers are buying the goods that China’s industries produce. Otherwise, everything else must be exported, often at lower prices. The leadership understands this in principle but believes that the control of advanced industries and technology will, ipso facto, cause productivity to rise, sustain economic growth into the future, and generate higher wages and therefore higher consumption.

This is the flaw in Beijing’s approach—the dangerous legacy of vestigial Marxism and misapplied neoclassical growth theory. In reality, state intervention in markets can depress overall productivity and workers can see flat wages even when China succeeds at promoting advanced industries.

It is true that capital and technology create productivity gains in well-functioning market economies. But the causality usually breaks down if resources are allocated by policy interventions that are divorced from returns on investment. The control or ownership of advanced industries does not inherently cause economic growth, because they are far too small a share of the economy. Instead, new products or technologies generate productivity when they are distributed and used throughout the economy in ways that improve efficiency or increase output. It is not the success of a robotics firm that leads to efficiency gains, for example, it is the deployment of its robots in factories to save production costs—namely by displacing workers—and boost output. If those benefits do not exceed the true cost of the new industrial robots—even with layers of subsidies—then the net effect is not positive, no matter how impressive the factories themselves are, or how successful the robotics firm itself appears.

The use of new production technologies also requires a degree of creative destruction that Beijing’s own industrial policy interventions have inhibited. When governments, not price-conscious firms, make technology and investment decisions, policymakers are not just gambling that they know better than the market how to boost long-run performance. They are also betting that they know how to use those technologies to create innovative new business models. Yet in China, state influence over resource allocation has ossified markets, especially by reducing bankruptcies, in ways that limit the fruits of innovation and efficiency gains in the broader economy. Additionally, much of China’s industrial policy aims to build self-reliance, which, by definition, focuses on duplicative investments that buttress domestic industrial prowess without necessarily adding efficiency.

Moreover, even though China’s many layers of industrial policy have helped launch successful companies and built an impressive fleet of ultramodern factories, there are also tremendous inefficiencies and waste that never make the headlines. Overall productivity must be calculated comprehensively, evaluating the net output gains against all the industrial subsidies, bad debts, foregone profits, and indirect support for investment that the government has provided. The reality is that China’s aggregate success rate is far lower than the shining stars would suggest: the remarkable global reach of electric vehicle and battery makers such as BYD, CATL, and Li Auto masks the dozens of failed companies that generated nonperforming loans and ate up unprofitable capital subsidies throughout the bulk of the sector and its supply chain. It is far from obvious that the net return on investment from industrial policy spending, estimated by the International Monetary Fund to be up to four percent of GDP, is positive, and it could be deeply negative, despite pockets of success.

Finally, Beijing is betting that superefficient manufacturing and success in strategic industries will eventually lead to higher wages, which will then cause consumption to surge. It is true that productivity growth causes real incomes to rise in a competitive market economy. But if investments in labor-saving technologies are driven by state policy, not returns on investment, wages can fall even as firms become more efficient. Rising household income requires a key intermediate step: employment, which is not a core characteristic of China’s capital-intensive, advanced manufacturing investment strategy. Indeed, state funding has helped China—a middle-income economy—become a world leader in high-tech “dark factories” that operate without distracting human accommodations, such as light. This may increase output in prized manufacturing cells in the input-output tables, but if demand for labor is not growing in aggregate, the whole equation starts to fall apart.

Still, the most pernicious consequence of Beijing’s economic model is entrenched deflation. The focus on expanding production combined with China’s weak consumer demand has caused the producer price index to fall for longer than it has risen over the past decade. This is a far larger threat to China’s economy than a mere nuisance of sectoral imbalances. Deflation reduces private-sector credit demand; undercuts incentives for new investments; and crushes employment, wage expectations, and, therefore, consumer confidence, which leads to weaker domestic demand—not in carefully demarcated input-output relationships but throughout the economy. Deflation also saps fiscal revenues and puts pressure on financial institutions in ways that severely limit the state’s capacity to act decisively the longer it lasts. Deflationary pressures in China also spill over to the global economy through cheaper exports and a weakening real exchange rate, driving more tensions between Beijing and its trading partners.

There is immense risk in falling behind the curve in fighting deflation, but Beijing is not likely to change course if it continues to believe its strategy will boost productivity and jumpstart domestic demand in the long run. Some analysts speculate that Beijing could be forced into a reappraisal of its vision in response to unemployment pressures or the proliferation of foreign trade friction, but it has already shown its cards. The accumulation of unemployment, underemployment, and low wages for Chinese households and workers are already significant, yet Beijing has responded with only modest new household subsidies and incremental investment in social services. Likewise, as external trade tensions have risen, Beijing has managed these country-by-country disputes as diplomatic issues, through a mix of threats and negotiations, to preserve the bulk of China’s export markets.

The decision to pursue short-term Band-Aid measures for a weak labor market and foreign trade tensions is confusing at first pass. For a government laser-focused on self-reliance and eliminating foreign dependencies, it is a curious strategy to become ever more dependent on foreign demand—over which Beijing has little control—as its primary driver of economic growth. Likewise, for a regime that is obsessed with social stability, it would seem prudent to focus more on wages and labor demand. Yet the strategy makes a degree of sense when viewed from the leadership’s perspective that China is in a transitional period. It may be unpleasant and difficult, but it is an unavoidable step on the path to a technology-led growth model.

The leadership’s current confidence in this transition process means that it could be many years before the warning signs, already visible, become persuasive internally. This all but guarantees that Beijing will continue to defer action while deflationary pressures and external trade tensions build. Deflation and weak corporate profitability are already eroding China’s fiscal revenues, which have basically been flat in nominal terms since 2019. Deflation and the growing debt burden are also corroding the financial system, which will ultimately require large write-offs and recapitalization from the government budget to prevent credit growth from slowing further. A $54 billion bank recapitalization just took place two months ago, with little effect on lending.

Beijing’s ideological commitment to its industry- and technology-focused development strategy is creating a dangerous cycle that will likely produce weaker consumption, slower income growth, and even greater trade friction with the rest of the world. Moreover, in the face of such challenges, China’s economic leadership is compensating by expanding state intervention in the economy in ways that further undermine market forces and the independence of the private sector. At this rate, even if the leadership eventually recognizes the need to change strategy, China may not have the fiscal or financial space to rebalance the economy toward a more sustainable and diversified growth model.

#5876. The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Review: The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

Loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, fled as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a new visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv.

They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name.

“You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge.

Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves—to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine.

Loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an art-house cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out.

Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta, where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, well-written articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she says. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.”

Alesya Marokhovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.”

Despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today.

Irina Dolinina continues to work in exile from Prague.Cinetic

The hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Important Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. New friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he says, not Russia.

But for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities.

Months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.”

Despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child.

You’d have to be fearless or a fanatic to persist in journalism in Russia. These women are both.

So-called realists arguing for Ukraine’s surrender can’t let go of the past.

How Moscow broke with the West—and unleashed a more chaotic world.

Ksenia Mironova and co-director Julia Loktev speak after a screening of My Undesirable Friends: Part II: Exile at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 27.Michael Loccisano/Getty Images

Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive.

Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years.

In the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful.

After leaving Russia with her family, Anna Nemzer spent time in Tblisi, Georgia.Cinetic

Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile. In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it.

Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-and-white tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom.

Or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, says tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.”

Valeria Ratnikova stays in a hotel in Istanbul after fleeing Russia.Cinetic

The only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his Fuck the War! podcast between missions.

From its new home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works.

For now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority.

One of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future.

Her writing has appeared in the Atlantic, the New York Review of Books, the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, Project Syndicate, and others. #5873. The New Congress Can Repair Civil-Military Relations

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

PETER D. FEAVER is Professor of Political Science and Public Policy at Duke University and the author of Thanks for Your Service: The Causes and Consequences of Public Confidence in the U.S. Military.

HEIDI URBEN is Professor of the Practice and Associate Director of Georgetown University’s Center for Security Studies in the Walsh School of Foreign Service.

How It Can Reclaim Its Constitutional Powers

Article I of the Constitution gives Congress sweeping powers to raise, maintain, and equip the armed forces. But the current Congress has done little to use these powers. The intense, frenetic activity of the past two years has undone established norms for military professionalism and may shape civil-military relations for a generation. Yet it has been led almost entirely by the executive branch with little meaningful involvement or pushback from Capitol Hill.

The next Congress will face great pressure to reverse course and in doing so could shore up the historical norms of American civil-military relations. The concern today is not a military that is defying civilians—the traditional bogeyman of American political leaders since the founding of the Republic. Rather, the fear is that the thousands of changes, large and small, that the executive branch has so rapidly imposed on the military may end up undermining the professional ethic on which the U.S. form of civilian control depends.

The incoming Congress can push U.S. civil-military relations in a healthier direction by overseeing the executive branch more actively than its predecessor. It can also help restore trust with both the military and the American public if it focuses on providing greater transparency, takes a more assertive role in conducting defense policy, reinforces the military’s nonpartisan professional ethic, and establishes a new bipartisan commission to reinvigorate the military profession. Congress has the power and authority to improve civil-military relations. The new session, starting in January, is its chance to use them before the damage becomes irreversible.

When Pete Hegseth was sworn in as defense secretary, in 2025, he had strong views on the changes he wanted to make, alleging the military had lost its warfighting focus because of misguided priorities and “wokeism.” He has pursued those changes with a zeal not seen since Robert McNamara held the office from 1961 to 1968. Hegseth has reshaped the senior officer ranks: he has fired or removed nearly two dozen senior general and flag officers, and he has gotten rid of more than one-quarter of all four-star generals, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the chiefs of the U.S. Air Force, Army, and Navy. He has fired, removed, or pulled from promotion lists approximately 80 general and flag officers, a disproportionate number of whom are women or racial minorities. Hegseth has justified those removals in the vaguest of terms, which has convinced most observers that the real reason amounts to little more than because these officers followed the lawful orders of the previous administration. No previous defense secretary has removed such large swaths of the officer corps who honored their oaths to the Constitution and faithfully implemented policies decided by their civilian superiors.

Hegseth has moved quickly, largely ignoring traditional bureaucratic practices, including rigorous staff reviews and close involvement of congressional stakeholders in changing the trajectory of the Pentagon’s policymaking and in conducting military operations. Amid ongoing questions about the legality of the boat strikes the Trump administration ordered against suspected drug traffickers last fall as well as civilian casualties in America’s war with Iran, it is critical to note that Hegseth had already fired the senior, most experienced military legal advisers—sending a warning shot across the bow of younger judge advocates—and begun a significant overhaul of the Judge Advocate General Corps. Ever since the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War, when U.S. soldiers committed war crimes by killing hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians, the JAG Corps had been empowered to help U.S. personnel abide by the laws of armed conflict. By demoting senior legal advisers and selecting less qualified personnel in those positions, however, the military’s legal voice is more marginalized today than it has been since the Vietnam War. The Trump administration has also centralized decision-making, including by placing routine actions in highly classified channels that minimize opportunities for input and deliberation.

Hegseth has done all of this—and much more—with essentially no pushback from the uniformed military or Pentagon bureaucracy. On the one hand, this shows just how strongly officers accept the principle of civilian control—a posture reinforced precisely because Hegseth has proved willing to punish even unsupported allegations of military insubordination. On the other hand, his actions have had a chilling effect across the force, creating an environment in which the military is reluctant to offer candid advice or uphold its professional standards and values when they are at odds with administration priorities. Indeed, in a highly unusual move, former government officials have publicly called for military leaders to do more to stand up to the Trump administration, even at the cost of undermining civilian control. As we argued in Foreign Affairs in 2024, however, the military cannot save democracy; only Congress and the courts can and should check presidential power.

Hegseth has enjoyed the unwavering support of President Donald Trump. But the real secret to Hegseth’s success in imposing his agenda on the Pentagon has been the unwillingness of the current Congress to exercise its Article I responsibilities or defend its traditional prerogatives. The incoming Congress can take a different approach by using its power to build trust, transparency, and accountability.

Most pressing, Congress should exercise its ability to appropriately scrutinize defense policymaking, much of which has been shrouded in secrecy under the Trump administration. The current Congress has held very few oversight hearings, and the ones that have taken place have been exchanges of insults rather than of information. When secrecy is genuinely needed, of course, Congress can issue classified briefings and hold closed hearings. But open hearings, when properly conducted, are necessary in cases in which Congress is entitled to answers, for example, about military personnel policy.

In the case of the boat strikes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific, Congress needs to know what advice senior military commanders and their JAGs offered, and it must understand how JAG firings affect the process by which commanders discern the lawfulness of military operations. Thus far, the Defense Department has provided only superficial explanations of its actions that basically amount to “we did this because we thought it was necessary.” Such justifications fall far short of what the Constitution envisions as the best way to hold the armed forces accountable: open debate that subjects policies to rigorous scrutiny. Greater transparency would also bolster public confidence in defense policy and remove pressure on the military to have to act as a potential savior of the Constitution.

Congress should also faithfully fulfill its “advice and consent” function established in Article II, which authorizes the Senate to review and confirm presidential nominations and promotions. Hegseth’s unprecedented intervention in the meritocratic promotion process has dramatically altered the military’s upper echelons. Congress has normalized this interference, perhaps unwittingly, by approving Hegseth’s altered promotion lists with voice votes and little inquiry.

The president and the defense secretary must retain the right to remove officers in whom they have lost confidence. But Congress has the right to know why a change was made, and it needs to ensure that promotions and removals follow established law and procedures rather than ideological or partisan considerations. Because Congress created the process for meritocratic promotions, it can push the executive branch to adhere to that process. It should mandate that the defense secretary provide a written explanation, supported by documented evidence of misconduct or derogatory information, for any off-cycle removals of senior officers and restore senior officers’ promotions, which would limit unjustified removals and uphold the merit-based selection process. Improving transparency in personnel policy will have one further salutary effect: it will help retain those qualified military personnel who are wondering whether they should give up on a military career that could be derailed by politicized and capricious promotion decisions.

In addition, Congress has a responsibility to police the well-established principle and practice that the uniformed military must stay away from partisan politics. The military has largely tried to uphold this norm, even as civilian political leaders have sought to draw it into partisan debates. Each time, for instance, Hegseth attacks the Biden administration before military audiences, most of whom served during the Biden era, he unwittingly further degrades the nonpartisan ethic on which service members’ oaths of office—and thus their subordination to his own policies—depend. It sends a message that embracing partisan rhetoric is key to career advancement and signals to the public that the military is not a neutral constituency. Congress can police the executive branch’s politicization of the military through inquiries, hearings, and even measures that prohibit the use of appropriated funds for events that treat military audiences like campaign rallies. Members of Congress can also call out for censure uniformed military personnel who behave in a blatantly partisan fashion regardless of whether they support or oppose the party the member supports.

Most ambitiously, Congress should reclaim its role in making defense policy rather than only providing oversight. Legislative deference to the executive in times of war is not unique to Trump’s second term, but Congress should close loopholes that allow presidents to expand their power unchecked. If Congress wants to provide a legal justification to allow the use of force in Iran or against drug traffickers in the Caribbean or the eastern Pacific Ocean, it should do so. If it believes these actions are unlawful, however, it must use its legislative powers to constrain them. Similarly, Congress should amend the Insurrection Act to clarify and restrict the domestic use of military force. The president must retain the ability to respond to true national emergencies, but Congress should narrow the criteria for deployment of troops on U.S. soil to avoid potential abuse.

Even as it becomes more active, Congress must strenuously avoid involving the military in a partisan war. Members of Congress should not press the military to criticize the president or the defense secretary in the made-for-social-media-outrage hearings that have become commonplace in Washington. It is right and proper for Congress to ask members of the military to share their personal and professional opinions on key strategic questions. But too often, politicians try to turn officers into combatants in their partisan battles, hiding behind the armed forces to defend partisan agendas or attacking military leaders who have simply carried out the lawful orders of a president from another party. Above all, Congress should not ask the military to be a check on civilian power. Only other civilians have the authority to do that.

Congress cannot solve longer-term issues through the day-to-day legislative process. But it has other tools to more holistically improve civil-military relations and identify the most essential reforms. The time-honored strategy is to set up a nonpartisan blue-ribbon commission to analyze problems, draw attention to their importance, and recommend solutions. A national commission on the state of the professional military ethic, co-chaired by three respected individuals—one with experience in a Republican administration, one with experience in a Democratic administration, and one retired senior military leader—would have the freedom to investigate how recent developments, including attempts to politicize the military and sustain a high tempo of operations, have affected the force. At a minimum, the commission should explore impacts on recruiting and retention; professional military education, fellowships in civilian institutions, and general and flag officer development; the JAG Corps’ ability to provide commanders with candid, independent legal advice; and the state of the National Guard.

The current Congress has not shown enough interest in exercising its own powers. The next one can make a clean break and rediscover the body’s ability to carry out the functions that are necessary to improve civil-military relations. The new Congress can demonstrate its commitment to fulfilling its responsibilities by providing ordinary legislative oversight in the raising, maintaining, and equipping of the armed forces. And on thorny issues that require a bigger response, Congress can start the reform process by creating a national commission to lay out an agenda for action. Even after two years of enormous strain that has eroded best practices in civil-military relations, the next Congress is well positioned to reverse the slide and shore up Americans’ faith in a nonpartisan, professional military that is essential to democracy.

#5872. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#5871. Realism Was Forged in Trauma

Review: Realism Was Forged in Trauma

Some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence. Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

This is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

Some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence. Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, David M. Sacks, Henry Holt & Co., 528 pp., $36.99, November 2026

This is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

The Realist starts with a cold open: summer 1922 in Coburg, Germany, on a day Morgenthau would later describe as the worst of his life. A high school junior ranked second in his class, Morgenthau was slated to address his peers as part of a celebratory academic tradition. “But what should have been a triumph quickly turned to humiliation,” writes Sacks. The townspeople turned their backs, spat on Morgenthau, and barraged him with antisemitic vitriol for having the gall to participate in a “Christian Day” ceremony. All because, in their eyes, he was no more than a “stinking Jew.”

While that day would leave an indelible scar on Morgenthau, it wasn’t his true awakening. Later that year, he would attend one of Hitler’s gatherings in Munich to witness with his own eyes the antisemitic tide said to be sweeping across all of Germany. It was “one of the most profound experiences of my life,” Morgenthau recalled. Soon after, the same scene played out in his own backyard: In defiance of local law, the führer sallied into Coburg with 800 stormtroopers and delivered two fiery philippics, whipping up a public paroxysm of threats, assaults, and mass street brawls, with tacit support from town police.

In just two days’ time, Morgenthau’s sleepy, parochial hometown became one of the Nazis’ earliest political proving grounds. From this, Morgenthau “drew a clear lesson,” writes Sacks. “He, and other powerless individuals, could not rely on the law or abstract ideals for protection.”

Nazis in Coburg, Germany, in 1922. Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

In one sense, The Realist is, as its title suggests, a study on an -ism—the school of thought that every international relations major must acquaint themselves with during their baptismal power-skim of Morgenthau’s 750-page syllabus staple, Politics Among Nations. The book sketches all the contours of political realism: Nations pursue power above all; peace depends on a healthy balance of it; and moral values must align with national interest and practical constraints.

But the basis of this framework, Sacks writes, was not incubated in an ivory tower; it was forged from a story of Sturm und Drang. Growing up Jewish during the rise of the Third Reich, Morgenthau endured a traumatic crescendo of antisemitism that “molded one’s whole life,” he wrote. He was the target of constant bullying and abuse, finding respite only in schoolwork, and sank into isolation and embitterment at a young age. Morgenthau’s father, too, was not spared: A doctor, he lost his medical license after the Nazis falsely accused him of professional misconduct, wiping away what little standing the family had left in Coburg.

After Morgenthau left for Frankfurt to pursue philosophy and law, he drew on the brutishness he’d seen among the common German volk—that “primitive” and “irrational” impulse—to elaborate his grand theory of power, one that was, in a sense, post-traumatic in character. It demanded constant hypervigilance and self-preservation. It doubted the durability of security commitments, and expressed a healthy skepticism toward rules, norms, and laws. And it saw the world’s default state as anarchy, ready to rear its ugly head yet again at any time. “The distribution of power,” as Morgenthau warned, “is always precarious.”

In the lead-up to World War II, this distribution of power wasn’t just skewing toward Germany; it was careening dangerously in Hitler’s favor. Few observers at the time saw this as lucidly—or as urgently—as Morgenthau, and Hitler’s expansionist designs were proof of concept.

But despite this prescience, it seems, Morgenthau mostly floundered as a young academic. He took whatever teaching jobs he could find in a Europe ravaged by the Great Depression with little appetite for his ideas, let alone his ethnic heritage. In Geneva, Sacks writes, colleagues found his Cassandra-like rhetoric a “disturbing influence.” At Brooklyn College, students felt his anticommunism was befitting of a hysterical “Hearst reporter.” In Kansas City, which Morgenthau called an “overgrown cow town,” his émigré ambition clashed with a culture in which academic standards were relatively modest—or, again in his words, “virtually non-existent.” Even when he first arrived at the tony University of Chicago, where he’d be a fixture for the next three decades, Morgenthau’s emphasis on theory over practice and empiricism put him at odds with his department.

The school of thought doesn’t explain everything—but its proponents foresaw the potential for conflict over Ukraine long before it erupted.

What emerges from this account is a portrait of a man who was not just politically persecuted but constantly intellectually embattled. Yet he was never cowed by power. By Morgenthau’s own admission, he refused “to play the role of the suffering martyr,” and it’s hard not to agree. The book makes clear that Morgenthau met nearly every criticism he faced with an equal and opposite reaction. This is someone who took to prestige media to publicly pillory his detractors with a revolutionary’s zeal (“trash,” “hatchet man,” “fanatical wrongheadedness”), as if their objections were affronts to his own lived experience.

And perhaps they were. After all, Sacks spills relatively little ink on the thinker’s life outside of work. In this respect, the book seems to imply by omission that Morgenthau’s personal and intellectual identities were, by dint of his traumatic upbringing, fused. We are teased with tidbits about Morgenthau’s wife, who softened his hard edges among friends and whose family supported them financially; his mother, the “closest companion throughout his life”; his authoritarian father, who believed he would never amount to anything; his son, who appeared to suffer from various ailments; and his extramarital affairs, which were far from passionless.

But for the most part, these read like brief digressions with little bearing on the bigger story. This is a weak point for a first-ever biography of such a fascinating figure, let alone one whose intellectual mission clearly seemed to color his personal life in a number of ways, and vice versa. Consider, for example, Morgenthau’s sudden interest in the Jewish question: The theorist had never been observant, did not know his Hebrew name, and was largely agnostic on Israel and the plight of the Soviet Jewry until his early 60s, believing that the Jewish state fell outside his sphere of interest. But by the late 1960s, after his forced retirement from the University of Chicago, Sacks writes, something “elemental” had shifted in Morgenthau. Feeling “disillusioned and cast aside,” he suddenly found great meaning and purpose in the Jewish community. His personal involvement with Chabad in particular fueled a political zeal for aiding Soviet refuseniks as well as a fierce insistence on Israel’s right to self-defense following the Six-Day War. This is a highly intriguing turn in Morgenthau’s story, but it’s, again, one The Realist gives little airtime.

Similarly, the book also could have lingered a bit more on Morgenthau’s bond with Hannah Arendt, another Jewish German émigré who fled the Nazis. The duo’s epistolary exchanges are rich with romantic intrigue—he may have proposed to her while still married—and intellectual compatibility. After all, they were both strangers in a strange land, hacking their way through the U.S. garden of liberal rationalism. When Arendt unveiled her infamous theory of the “banality of evil” while covering Adolf Eichmann’s trial in 1963, she provoked an intellectual maelstrom among colleagues at the University of Chicago, many of whom shunned her in response. Morgenthau, meanwhile, stood by Arendt and wrote to her gushingly, “Reality has protruded into the protective armor of illusion and the result is psychological havoc.” His use of the word “reality” was likely no coincidence.

Morgenthau addresses an audience in Washington, D.C., on May 15, 1965, while taking part in a national, 15-hour teach-in on the Vietnam War.Associated Press

Over the past several years, conflicts from Gaza to Ukraine to Iran have prompted a great deal of debate among observers about whether the world is seeing the supposed return of realism. However, it’s worth remembering that aggression alone is not a good proxy for the presence of realism, which, as John Mearsheimer notes, is in large part predicated on restraint. Rather, the violence exposes a core realist truth: With no mechanism of holding great powers to account, the international rules-based order is still only as strong as those who abide by it.

The Realist, for its part, wisely avoids wading into contemporary politics, instead letting the resonance of realism’s history speak for itself. Nowhere is that more striking than in the book’s account of the Vietnam War.

One might assume that Morgenthau—who called for a very muscular posture toward the Soviet-backed Castro government during the Cuban missile crisis—was all for U.S. intervention in communist North Vietnam. However, Sacks goes to great lengths to show that he was an outspoken opponent from the jump: For two decades, Morgenthau waged a war of words with officials in the Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon administrations, including McGeorge Bundy, Robert McNamara, Walt Rostow, and Henry Kissinger (a frenemy of sorts). By the mid-1960s, as the conflict became clearly unwinnable, Morgenthau grew deeply distressed by the carnage on moral grounds. But his original argument had always been one of narrow political strategy: that the growth of communism in North Vietnam “simply was not a vital interest,” as Sacks writes. We must only intervene “where our national interest requires it and where our power gives us a chance to succeed,” Morgenthau wrote. “If the United States applies this standard, it will intervene less and succeed more.”

To say that the United States has done just the opposite would be a great understatement. In the aftermath of 9/11, President George W. Bush’s anti-terror war in Iraq created the conditions for the world’s deadliest terror organization to flourish, while the war in Afghanistan—which spanned four presidents—began and ended with Taliban rule. Though U.S. officials justified both interventions on the basis of national interest, prominent members of the neorealist school vehemently opposed them. Broadly speaking, this was because the conflicts were driven less by narrow strategy and more by either quixotic (nation-building) or chimeric (eliminating weapons of mass destruction) goals. When those goals could not be realized, the U.S. mission crept, and officials resorted to sunk-cost fallacies about credibility instead of retrenchment; the very same tack was taken by Kissinger, who attempted to argue on realist grounds that the United States would lose international “prestige” by pulling out of Vietnam. As for the current war in Iran, declared on the all-too-familiar pretext of imminent nuclear capability, the United States seems woefully bound to repeat the same cycle, and no amount of victory declarations from our commander-in-chief will change that.

To be sure, these military misadventures do not suggest that realism reigns supreme in international relations. Instead, they point to one of its key weaknesses: the malleability of “national interest”—especially, and perhaps ironically, in the face of trauma.

When Morgenthau published his first book, Scientific Man versus Power Politics, in 1946, Sacks notes that some critics found the term “national interest” too nebulous—a gripe that Morgenthau actually took in stride. U.S. military misadventures in the Middle East reveal that this problem remains in full effect. The country’s collective trauma after 9/11 gave the U.S. government a pretext to widen the aperture of “national interest” so much so that temporally or geographically distant threats—like simmering political instability in a region many Americans could not point to on a map—suddenly became existentially urgent. “As long as the Middle East remains a place where freedom does not flourish,” as Bush said in 2003, “it will remain a place of stagnation, resentment, and violence ready for export.” The United States met this specter of violence in much the same way it did Vietnam’s communism: with real violence. After two decades, our efforts to install a democratic regime resulted in nothing more than hundreds of thousands of civilian casualties. “The evil we wanted to prevent,” as Morgenthau wrote of Vietnam, was “nothing compared with the evil we left behind.”

It may be tempting to see the “return” of realism in a world where the United States continues to pursue power brutally, by any means necessary. Yet if realist thought now predominates among U.S. foreign-policymakers, it is a far cry from the realism of Morgenthau’s making. Instead, it is a realism in which national trauma has turned national interest into an empty signifier, used for vengeful wish fulfillment at the expense of sober statecraft. If “great nations” like the United States are truly great because “they married … power to purpose,” as Morgenthau believed, then what has that purpose been over the last quarter-century of foreign policy? It’s hard to think of anything other than power itself.

#5869. Dems campaign promise to freeze energy costs faces glaring reality check

Sam Romain, chairman of Americans for Energy Dominance, believes Democrats will have no choice but to grapple with supply-side policy challenges once their commitments stall

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is preparing her first step into left-leaning policies in the historically deep red state by implementing an emergency utility rate freeze — but one expert worries the proposal will become a failed attempt to address the affordability crisis.

More Democratic-led states are looking to impose similar plans to Hinojosa's after she said on Day One of being governor that she will freeze residential electricity rates, an idea that many warn clashes with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector and could inadvertently create energy shortages.

"It's a campaign promise they made on the trail," Sam Romain, chairman of the free market group Americans for Energy Dominance, told Fox News Digital. "But they don't have the power to just freeze the rates. You can't just wave a magic wand and freeze the rates."

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa speaks to members of the media during a block walk campaign event in San Antonio, Texas, on Nov. 1, 2026. (Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Romain believes it’s only a matter of time before Democrats across the country have to wrestle with ways to increase energy production — even as they are currently exploring a variety of energy price controls.

"We know that price works based on supply and demand, right? It's basic, basic economics," Romain said.

"And what you're seeing across the nation is this Democratic price control scheme that's dressed up as an emergency. The problem is you can't necessarily freeze your way out of the supply problems," Romain added.

Some Democratic-led strategies aim to lock down energy prices while others look to subsidize them. Some plans call for both.

In one such case, Democrat Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who took office in January, is demanding a six-year rate freeze as a Florida company looks to buy Virginia’s largest energy supplier. She has also called for "a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers."

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill promised to declare a state of emergency to cap energy rates at the outset of her term in January 2026, but has since pivoted to implement a credit system to offset electricity costs using executive orders.

Among the newly elected Democrats, California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to "institute a freeze on utility rates… while the state investigates long-term solutions to bring these costs under control," a strategy he framed as a priority.

In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley will lead a legislature that last year entertained a proposal to cap gas and electricity bills at 4% of a qualifying household’s annual income. Crowley himself has also proposed a similar "fair deal" plan that would cap annual rent increases at 7%.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger pushed her party to pass the ballot initiative. (Maxine Wallace/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

And in Ohio, Democratic state leadership led by House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn has proposed a 12-month freeze on utility rates as Amy Acton prepares to take the gubernatorial mansion.

To Romain, these proposals deal a twofold blow.

In addition to failing to build out supply, he believes they also discourage additional production. "A freeze in and of itself doesn't actually build anything. Actually, it does almost the opposite. It discourages developers from building. They don't know if they're going to be able to recoup their profit margin on their construction," Romain said.

Questions also remain about the legality of some of the plans. In Texas, for instance, experts have noted that Hinojosa’s planned use of an emergency declaration may quickly run into legal resistance.

Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy, questioned the emergency powers Hinojosa says she plans to use.

"The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts, but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris said.

Romain believes Democrats will face similar legal hurdles in other states. But even though he expects price-control strategies to stall, Romain believes that creates an opportunity: fertile ground for a bipartisan affordability strategy as Democrats look to keep their commitments.

"Democrats know there's a supply-side issue," Romain said.

LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN

Gov. Mikie Sherrill speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton on March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Their solution to it is different than the Republicans'… And the solution is quite simply to just let American companies build and compete. The problem is to unleash American innovation. This country was built by builders, right? And so let our companies build the tools they need, let them build the generation sites, let them build the power plants," Romain said.

Permitting reform is one area in particular he believes may soon turn into an area for cooperation, a deregulation of the rules that govern energy production.

"I'm actually really optimistic… that we're going to have a massive permit reform package done very quickly, very soon, actually," Romain said.

"I think that we have a massive opportunity in front of us."

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

#5868. The EU’s First AI Summit
